subtitle: A systematic approach to understanding songs through music theory

introduction.title: Why Analyze Songs?
introduction.text: Most guitarists learn songs by memorizing finger positions from tablature. While this gets you playing quickly, it doesn't help you understand why the song works or how to apply those concepts to other music. Our analysis method transforms you from a tab-reader into a musician who understands the language of music. You'll learn to recognize patterns, predict chord changes, and even improvise over songs you've never heard before.

cards.title: Identify the Key Center
cards.description: The key is your musical "home base" - the note that feels like resolution. Most songs start and end on their key center, and the bass notes often outline it.
items: Listen to the first and last chords (often the key center)
Identify the bass note that feels like "home"
Look for the chord that provides the strongest resolution
Check the key signature if sheet music is available

cards.title: Map the Chord Progression
cards.description: Convert chord names to Roman numerals based on the key. This reveals the harmonic function and makes patterns visible across different keys.
items: I-V-vi-IV (Pop progression) - C-G-Am-F in key of C
I-IV-V (Classic rock) - E-A-B in key of E
vi-IV-I-V (Ballad progression) - Am-F-C-G in key of C
ii-V-I (Jazz standard) - Dm-G-C in key of C

cards.title: Analyze Song Structure
cards.description: Break the song into sections and understand how they function together. Each section typically has a specific harmonic and melodic purpose.
items: Intro: Sets mood, often hints at main progression
Verse: Tells the story, usually more subdued harmonically
Pre-Chorus: Builds tension toward the chorus
Chorus: Main hook, strongest harmonic resolution
Bridge: Provides contrast, often uses different chords
Outro: Concludes the song, often returns to intro material

cards.title: Identify Scales and Modes
cards.description: Determine which scales work over each section. Most pop/rock uses major or minor pentatonic, but understanding modes opens up more sophisticated options.
items: Major Key Songs: Major pentatonic, major scale, Mixolydian mode
Minor Key Songs: Minor pentatonic, natural minor, Dorian mode
Bluesy Songs: Blues scale, minor pentatonic with blue notes
Modal Songs: Match the mode to the tonal center

cards.title: Break Down Rhythm Patterns
cards.description: Analyze the strumming patterns, picking techniques, and rhythmic feel. The rhythm is often what defines the genre and groove of a song.
items: Time signature (4/4, 3/4, etc.)
Strumming pattern (down/up strokes)
Tempo and feel (straight, swing, shuffle)
Accent patterns and dynamics
Palm muting and articulation
Syncopation and off-beat emphasis

cards.title: Catalog Guitar Techniques
cards.description: Identify specific guitar techniques used and understand how they serve the music. This builds your technical vocabulary and shows you when to use each technique.
items: Chord types (open, barre, power)
Lead techniques (bends, slides, vibrato)
Picking styles (alternate, economy, hybrid)
Special effects (harmonics, tapping)
Fingerpicking patterns
Capo usage and open tunings

cards.title: Analyze Tone and Effects
cards.description: Understanding the gear and effects used helps you recreate the sound and teaches you how different tones serve different musical purposes.
items: Guitar Type: Solid-body, hollow-body, acoustic
Pickup Selection: Bridge, neck, middle positions
Amplification: Tube, solid-state, modeling
Effects: Distortion, reverb, delay, modulation
EQ Settings: Bass, mid, treble adjustments

sections.title: Example: Quick Analysis
sections.introText: Let's apply this method to a simple example. Consider the classic progression: C - Am - F - G

cards.title: Analysis Walkthrough
numberedItems: Key Center: C major (C chord feels like home)
Progression: I - vi - IV - V (very common pop progression)
Structure: Could be a verse or chorus progression
Scale: C major scale or C major pentatonic work perfectly
Rhythm: Depends on the song, but often strummed in 4/4
Technique: Open chords, simple strumming pattern
Tone: Clean or lightly driven acoustic/electric guitar
cards.description: This analysis immediately tells you that you can use C major pentatonic for lead lines, that this progression will sound good in any key when transposed, and that it follows a predictable harmonic pattern found in thousands of songs.

cards.title: Start Simple
items: Begin with 3-chord songs
Focus on major keys first
Use songs you already know well
Practice identifying just the key center initially

cards.title: Build Gradually
items: Add one analysis step at a time
Keep a song analysis journal
Compare similar songs to find patterns
Practice with different genres

cards.title: Use Technology
items: Slow down audio to hear details
Use apps to identify chords
Record yourself playing progressions
Loop sections for detailed study

cards.title: Apply Your Knowledge
items: Transpose songs to different keys
Write your own songs using common progressions
Improvise over backing tracks
Teach others what you've learned

relatedTopics.title: Ready to Start Analyzing?
relatedTopics.description: Now that you understand the method, it's time to put it into practice. Start with our structured song breakdowns to see this approach in action, then apply it to your own favorite songs.
